chunks.text: Every emergency system we rely on shares one assumption.
That the network will still be there.
When the power fails, the towers go quiet. The alert never arrives. The call never connects. And the people who most need to be found disappear from the map.
January twenty twenty-six. Adamuz, southern Spain. A train derails at night.
According to the published timeline, the first emergency call came within about a minute.
But it took around forty-five minutes for responders to learn that a second train was down. The first report carried only one set of coordinates.
Hundreds of phones were on board. Each one knew something. Nothing connected them.
This is not one failure. It is a structural gap.
Public alerts depend on the cellular network. Professional radio connects responders, not citizens.
Navigation apps react after the road is already blocked. And no one forecasts where people will be left in the dark.
This is SENDA.
If a path to your people exists, SENDA finds it.

scenes.title: The router: every channel at once

chunks.text: SENDA treats an emergency as a routing problem across time.
Bluetooth. Wi-Fi between phones. LoRa. S M S. A neighbour's satellite internet. A satellite passing overhead. Even sound.
Using contact graph routing, the technique designed for delay-tolerant space networks, it computes the earliest arrival through any chain of contacts, and launches several routes in parallel.
In our reference scenario, a town loses its antenna for eight hours. The conventional messenger delivers after four hundred and eighty minutes. SENDA, in simulation, delivers in about four.
And when no path exists, it does not invent one.

scenes.title: Delivery assurance: a number you can check

chunks.text: Channels do not fail one by one. In a storm or a blackout, they fail together.
A planner that assumes independence promises ninety-nine point five percent, and in our simulation delivers ninety-six.
SENDA's delivery assurance engine models those common causes, splits each message into fragments across channels that do not fall together, and reaches close to ninety-nine percent at no extra cost.
And every signed delivery receipt will teach it. That learning, zone by zone, is the data advantage we are building.
When an authority issues an alert, or public seismic catalogues confirm an event, an emergency zone is declared.
Phones whose owners agreed in advance become relays, within battery and data limits they control.
Every message travels in a signed, end-to-end encrypted envelope. Relays carry it. They cannot read it.
Go back to that night. Each phone detects the impact, and asks its owner one question. Are you all right?
No answer is also an answer. It is the signal rescuers need most.
SENDA fuses hundreds of reports into one picture: how many trains, which coaches, who is trapped.
In our simulations, the second train is identified in thirty to forty-one seconds. Even when only five percent of passengers have the app.

scenes.title: Under the rubble: the building twin

chunks.text: After an earthquake, every building becomes a question.
SENDA builds a digital twin from open map data. Floor by floor. Home by home.
A phone on the surface becomes a bridge for a phone below. Signal strength, measured as a rescuer walks, narrows the search and projects it onto the camera view.
And with a low-cost Wi-Fi sensor, our models detect breathing behind a wall. Today, on synthetic signals. Field calibration is the next step.

scenes.title: Fire, smoke and the evacuation corridor

chunks.text: Wildfires now outrun the systems built to manage them.
SENDA couples established physics: Rothermel fire spread, smoke dispersion, and traffic flow as a fluid.
So it can model how smoke cuts visibility, how a shock wave of stopped vehicles forms, and when a corridor will close.
And it forecasts which antennas the fire will reach, so the mesh is ready before the blackout.

scenes.title: The command view: real data, clearly labelled

chunks.text: For coordinators, one view. A four-dimensional globe, built on real open data.
Earthquakes from U S G S. Fires from NASA and Copernicus. Weather forecasts from MET Norway. Real terrain. Real road incidents.
Radio links are modelled over that terrain with international propagation standards, and drone survey routes are planned across it.
Every layer is labelled for what it is. Observation. Forecast. Or simulation. Never confused.
What makes this science is not a slogan. It is reproducibility.
{core} automated tests in the core, all passing. {e2e} end-to-end checks in a real browser, with the network switched off. Every figure on this screen is regenerated by running the code.
We publish our prior art. We do not claim to be first. We claim that our combination of routing, physics and evidence is implemented, measured, and open to inspection.
It is built on open standards and open data. And it runs on the phones people already carry.
Here is exactly where we stand. SENDA is a research-stage platform.

Its algorithms are proven in software and simulation. Phone-to-phone delivery, satellite links and through-wall sensing are not yet validated in the field. It is not connected to emergency services. And it must not be used in a real emergency today.
We tell you this first, because trust is the product.
One engine. Many fields.
Rail and transport operators. Civil protection and emergency centres. Wildfire and evacuation planning.
Road authorities and smart corridors. Urban search and rescue. Critical infrastructure that must keep talking when everything else stops.
What comes next is validation.
A field pilot with civil protection: a stopped train, fifty to one hundred volunteers, and one number to measure. The time until every coach is known.
A structured gateway to emergency centres. Native background apps. An independent security audit.
That is what your investment builds.
The network will fail again. The question is what happens in the silence.
SENDA. If a path exists, we find it.
